title: Hymnals
hook: the book in the pew held a people's theology

segments.voice: Yesterday, writing icons, made with prayer at the board. Your line was painting as prayer. What did you do slowly with your hands? Day one thousand three hundred sixty-four.

The pew in front of you has a slot cut into its back. In the slot, a thick book with a cracked spine and a faded cloth cover. Open it and somebody's pencil has marked a page. A funeral program is tucked in at another. The paper is thin, the print is small, and every page has lines of music above the words. Nobody would call it a theology book. It has no arguments, no footnotes. And yet a grandmother who never read a word of theology can sing half of it from memory, and in those songs is much of what her church believes about God, sin, grace and heaven. Today: hymnals.
screen: `A SLOT IN THE BACK OF THE PEW.`

segments.voice: Start with the Gospels. After the last supper, Matthew says, "And when they had sung an hymn, they went out into the mount of Olives." Jesus's last evening with his friends ends with a song. And in Acts, Paul and Silas sit in a prison with their feet in the stocks: "And at midnight Paul and Silas prayed, and sang praises unto God: and the prisoners heard them." Singing in the dark, with an audience. Next, why sing at all. Paul writes to the Colossians: "Let the word of Christ dwell in you richly in all wisdom; teaching and admonishing one another in psalms and hymns and spiritual songs, singing with grace in your hearts to the Lord." Look where singing sits in that sentence. Under teaching. A hymn isn't only a feeling set to a tune. It's a lesson that gets into your memory through the back door. Then, the book. A hymnal gathers what a church wants its people to carry. Martin Luther's hymn, in one old English version, opens: "A mighty fortress is our God, a bulwark never failing." That's a whole teaching about trust, in one line you can sing on the way home. Each church picks its own hymns, so a hymnal tells you what that church holds dear. Not every church uses one. Orthodox churches sing hymns from their service books, and some newer churches put the words up on a screen. The habit underneath is the same. Last, one line of Isaac Watts: "When I survey the wondrous cross, on which the Prince of glory died." The Prince of glory, dying. That line is a whole doctrine about who was on the cross. And people sing it without a footnote. That's the hymnal's quiet job: theology in song.
screen: `THEY SANG A HYMN, AND WENT OUT.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: read a hymn. Settle, and breathe. If you have a favorite, bring it to mind. If not, the screen has the opening verse of Isaac Watts's hymn. Read it slowly, once, the way you'd read a letter. Then read it again and ask one question of each line: what does this say about God? Don't try to sing it. Just let the words land one at a time. If you pray, you can let the last line be your prayer. If you don't, notice which line you'd remember tomorrow, and why. The bell holds the time.
screen: `WHEN I SURVEY THE WONDROUS CROSS, ON WHICH THE PRINCE OF GLORY DIED, MY RICHEST GAIN I COUNT BUT LOSS, AND POUR CONTEMPT ON ALL MY PRIDE.`

segments.voice: Hymnals. The book of a church's songs, and of what it believes, carried in memory more than on a shelf.
Your line: theology in song. Today, when a song gets stuck in your head, any song, listen to what it's teaching you about the world. Day one thousand three hundred sixty-four.

howItsDone: In Protestant and Catholic churches a hymnal often sits in the pews and the congregation sings from it together; Orthodox churches sing hymns from their service books, and some newer churches project the words on a screen instead.

myth: the New Testament never mentions singing hymns
Matthew says Jesus and his friends sang a hymn after supper, and Paul and Silas sang in prison.
"teaching and admonishing one another in psalms and hymns and spiritual songs."
every church sings from a hymnal in the pew
Orthodox churches sing from service books, and some newer churches put the words on a screen.

fork.setup: the last supper is over. before Jesus and his friends go out to the mount of Olives, what does Matthew say they do?
fork.reveal: "and when they had sung an hymn, they went out into the mount of Olives." the last evening ends with a song.

original.note: Greek: a song of praise. Colossians names hymns alongside psalms and spiritual songs.

trapdoor: what you thought: a hymnal is just a songbook.
what it means: a church's beliefs set to tunes, so people carry them by heart.
what a scholar hears: Colossians puts singing under teaching, "teaching and admonishing one another in psalms and hymns." the song is a lesson.
recall: Catholic and Orthodox word for it

notes: Editor pass: replaced the 'you're Paul' fork, which repeated day 1362's Paul fork, with a fork on the hymn after the last supper; swapped that match pair for Luther's hymn so the two games don't overlap.
Hedge's English version of Luther's hymn is 19th-century and public domain; quoted as commonly printed ('A mighty fortress is our God, a bulwark never failing'). Confirm punctuation.

Watts verse quoted with modern capitalization and punctuation; Watts's first printing reportedly read 'Where the young Prince of Glory died', later revised to the familiar line. Confirm the wording used.
Watts's hymn is often dated to 1707 in Hymns and Spiritual Songs; the date is not stated in the lesson. Confirm the source title in sources.
Hook scene (grandmother who sings from memory) is illustrative, not a claim.
'Orthodox churches sing hymns from their service books, and some newer churches put the words up on a screen': confirm fair and unquantified.
howItsDone says a hymnal often sits in the pews in Protestant and Catholic churches; confirm.
